title: EyeMatics - Eye Diseases “Treated” with Interoperable Medical Informatics
summary:
In Germany, around 10,000 new cases of blindness occur every year, which corresponds to an incidence of 12.3 per 100,000 inhabitants per year. Age-related macular degeneration alone accounts for 50% of blindness and diabetic retinopathy for 17%. The probability of suffering from one of these eye diseases increases significantly with age. As a result of increasing life expectancy, the number of blind or visually impaired people will also increase and the need for ophthalmic care will rise.
What these eye diseases have in common is that they can be treated with intravitreal injections (IVI). With intravitreal injections, a medication is administered directly into the vitreous body of the eye. The aim is to maintain or improve vision. Furthermore, IVI is the most common medical procedure in Germany and is performed around 1,000,000 times a year.
The injections must be carried out several times, usually between five and nine times per year per patient. However, the strategies for the best possible treatment intervals have not yet been sufficiently investigated outside of clinical studies (i.e. in the “real world”). The situation within our consortium with regard to different treatment regimens is exemplary for Germany: at the university hospitals in Tübingen and Münster, IVI treatments are generally planned in series of three consecutive injections according to the so-called pro-re-nata regimen, while in Greifswald and Aachen, some IVI patients are treated according to the treat-and-extend regimen with single injections and individually adapted treatment intervals.
Initial practical evaluations have shown that treatment outcomes in Germany do not match the published good study results, while patient outcomes in other countries such as the UK and France appear to be significantly better. In Germany, there is a lack of multi-center data collection of real treatment data that would allow a detailed analysis and thus improved patient care.
The aim of the “EyeMatics” project is therefore to make clinical data from patients with common eye diseases who receive IVI therapy available for scientific evaluation in order to improve patient care. To this end, EyeMatics combines individual data sources from various inpatient and outpatient care systems and makes this wealth of data accessible across all locations.
Treatment data from four university hospitals and two rollout partners will be extracted from the respective primary hospital systems and diagnostic devices in order to analyze them in a standardized data model. The project is an extension of the existing work of the Medical Informatics Initiative, which aims to make data from patient care and research more usable in order to strengthen research and improve care.
The added value of this project is that, for the first time, clinical data from the “real world” generated at various locations can be analyzed in the context of ophthalmology. In addition, patients are actively involved through the collection of patient-reported outcomes. The combined data will be analyzed with regard to various demographic and clinical parameters, treatment data, state-of-the-art imaging and treatment patterns. Clinical treatment data and examination images are analysed using artificial intelligence in order to identify new characteristic features and create the basis for personalized medicine in ophthalmology.
A clinical dashboard (web application) will be introduced as a demonstrator system at each location as an example of meaningful data processing and use in the healthcare context. This connects previously separate IT systems and visualizes real-time data across locations. This accelerates the identification of high-risk patients and the development of new, customized clinical guidelines in ophthalmology to an unprecedented extent.

interventions.name: Real treatment data of patients receiving IVI therapy will be analyzed in this study. There is no intervention as part of the study.
